lines: ARBITRATOR:  Thank you very much.
Good morning, everyone.
Thank you very much for joining.
My name is Karim Nassif.  I'm the sole arbitrator
in this ICC case number 29317/KFH, between Johnson
Controls Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Qatar WLL
as claimant, and Microsoft QSTP-LLC as respondent.
We have a long day.  I don't have much on the
housekeeping issues.  I have only two matters, quick.
I've just noticed that I haven't probably signed yet
the hearing protocol I'll be doing for today and send
it to you for your record.  Thank you very much for
signing it.
The second point is that I received yesterday the
errata of the witness statements from both sides.
Please ensure that those go to the hearing bundle as
well.  They are on my record.  They form part of the
record, of course, but please change them in the
hearing bundle so we can have the accurate hearing
bundle.
MS EID:  We've already changed.
ARBITRATOR:  Thank you.  Ms Hage, do you have any
housekeeping issues before we start?
MS HAGE:  On the claimant's side, no, sir.  Thank you.
ARBITRATOR:  Mr Roshan, on the respondent side?
MS ROSHAN:  Nothing for the respondent.  Thank you.
ARBITRATOR:  Thank you very much.  Who is taking the
times from both sides?
MS ROSHAN:  For the respondent, we have our team keeping
time and what we suggest.  I think this is also in the
protocol, that the claimant does the same.  And then
if there are any issues we can take that to the
tribunal.
ARBITRATOR:  Thank you.
MS HAGE:  Yes, this is confirmed.
ARBITRATOR:  Thank you very much, Ms Hage, shall we start
with your opening statement?
MS HAGE:  Yes.  Thank you.  My colleague Myriam Eid will
be doing the opening statements.  Thank you.
ARBITRATOR:  Yes.  Thank you very much, Ms Eid.  We are
all hearing you.  Thank you very much.
Opening submissions by MS EID
MS EID:  Good morning, Mr Nassif.
This case begins and concludes with a single
document, Microsoft's notice of breach addressed to
Intaleq on 29 March 2020, for which respondent itself
has put before this tribunal as evidence that it
fulfilled its obligations as the prime contractor.
We invite the tribunal to keep that document
firmly in mind throughout this process because it
exposes the contradiction at the heart of Microsoft's
case.
When Microsoft wrote to its customer, it took a
clear position.  It told Intaleq that Johnson Controls
has performed its obligation.  It demanded payment
from Johnson Controls work, the same sum Johnson
Controls now seeks in this arbitration, and it accused
Intaleq of breaching the contract by refusing to pay.
Yet today Microsoft asked the tribunal to find
that those same works were never completed and that
Johnson Controls is not entitled to payment.  Those
two positions cannot both be true.  Microsoft cannot
rely on Johnson Controls' performance when seeking
payment from Intaleq and deny that same performance
when Johnson Controls seeks payment from Microsoft.
And these contradictions runs even deeper,
Mr Nassif.  Johnson's case is straightforward.  It's a
straightforward payment claim for works performed
under amendment number 8, dated 19 December 2022,
which incorporated change order number 37.
The timing matters.  Amendment number 8 was signed
only after the FIFA World Cup in Qatar had concluded
on 18 December 2022.
Johnson Controls seeks in the arbitration payment
of 9.8 million Qatari riyals, comprising 7.4 million
for nine specific completed milestones, 2.3 in
contractual retention monies, out of which 1.5 relates
to certified unpaid milestones.
The tribunal will see that CR 37 leaves little
room for uncertainty.  In particular, table 2 and 10
define the revised scope of Johnson Controls.  Table 4
prescribes the acceptance criteria for milestone
performance, and table 5 sets out Microsoft's Intaleq,
obligations and dependencies.
The scope under CR 37 deletes and replaces the
original statement of work.  Accordingly, Microsoft's
reliance on pre-amendment number 8 issues to
justify --
ARBITRATOR:  One second, Ms Eid.
Muhammad, I just noticed that I have "AI meeting"
from my computer attending as well.
Can you please remove it from attendance?
TECHNICIAN:  Yes, sir.
ARBITRATOR:  Yes.  Thank you.  Sorry for that.  Thank you
very much.
Sorry for interrupting you, but I didn't wish to
have any AI recording anything else.  Thank you.
TECHNICIAN:  Yes, sir.  I confirm, removed now.
MS EID:  Mr Nassif, just confirming, you can hear me now?
ARBITRATOR:  Yes, madam.  We can hear you.
We are all yours.  Sorry for the interruption.
Thank you.
MS EID:  No worries.
So the tribunal will see that CR 37 leaves little
room for uncertainty.  In particular, tables 2 and 10
define the revised scope of Johnson Controls' work.
Table 5 prescribes the acceptance criteria for
milestone performance.  Table 4 sets out Microsoft and
Intaleq's obligations and dependencies.  The scope
under CR 37 deletes and replaces the original scope of
work.  Accordingly, Microsoft's reliance on
pre-amendment number 8 issues to justify nonpayment is
fundamentally inconsistent with amendment number 8
itself.
Amendment number 8 reset the parties' contractual
relationship, defined the revised scope of work
milestones and acceptance mechanism.  Against that
contractual framework the case turns on a single
question: did the CR 37 milestone become payable under
the agreed acceptance mechanism?  Clause 10 of
schedule 1 read together with section 5.4 of exhibit A
establishes a clear contractual acceptance mechanism.
It places Microsoft as prime contractor under the
obligation to secure the customer's acceptance of each
completed milestone and in case of rejection,
ensure -- and I quote:
"The end customer includes a complete list of
reasons for rejection."
Not just any reasons, they had to be specific,
milestone by milestone reasons tied to the agreed
acceptance criteria set out in CR 37.
Those same provisions expressly state that the
milestone is considered accepted, and becomes payable
upon the occurrence of one of three events.  Express
acceptance, deemed acceptance where no rejection
notice is issued by Microsoft within three business
days of submission, or the customer's actual, even
partial use of the deliverables.
The outstanding CR 37 milestones were submitted
for acceptance on 25 December 2022.  No rejection
notice was issued by Microsoft within the contractual
period or at any time thereafter while the customer
made actual use and is still using the solution.
Indeed, even in these proceedings, Microsoft has
failed to identify a single CR 37 milestone that was
or could probably have been rejected by reference to
the applicable acceptance criteria set out in CR 37.
As the evidence will show, both acceptance
requirements are satisfied in this case.  No rejection
of the specific milestones was issued, not at any
time, not at all.  The customer made and is still
making use of the solution.  Indeed, on 30 March 2023,
Microsoft issued the project's closure report to the
customer signed by Mr Beer, confirming that the
relevant milestones had been successfully completed in
accordance with CR 37.  And here, could I please ask
Muhammad to display {E84} from the bundle.
This is {E84}.
{E85}, please.
Mr Nassif, as you can see from page 1 of this
document, this is the final delivery report issued by
Microsoft prepared by Mr Beer, witness in this
arbitration.
Muhammad, can you please scroll down.
As you can see -- please, also down to the tables.
As you can see throughout this report, you will
see that all the scope of amendment number 8, CR 37 is
completed and all the defects are closed.  Table 2 and
10 specifically relate to claimant scope.  And if you
scroll down you will see that these two are completed.
This is table 2 completed.  Completed.
Please go down.
Thank you.  Completed.
Thank you.  I'm done with the document.  Thank
you.
Microsoft issued disclosure report which
identifies each item of claimant's scope as
successfully completed, defects as closed, and then
immediately revoked Johnson's access to the solution
on the same day, confirming the closure of the
project.
Then, on 1 June 2023, two months after closure,
Microsoft shared with Johnson Controls the so-called
gaps report.
The tribunal will hear considerable reliance
placed on this document by Microsoft to justify
failure to pay.  Yet the document, and, more
importantly, Microsoft's own contemporaneous
annotation on it, tell a very different story.
Microsoft notes, And please, Muhammad, could you
please display {E90}, page 10 on the screen.  These
are Mr Beer's annotations and feedback on Intaleq
statements in the gaps report.
As you can see from the third paragraph in blue,
Mr Beer's response to Intaleq comments were as
follows.  The solution was tested by Intaleq and
approved to be moved to production on
29 December 2022, and the non-event support started on
1 October.
The UNISTAD solution was heavily promoted by
Intaleq throughout the World Cup.  The data gathered
from the stadiums was collected and presented to
Intaleq through the BI dashboards.
Thank you, Muhammad.
Those contemporaneous statements are highly
significant.  They are not Johnson Controls' words.
They are Microsoft's own contemporaneous comments on
the very document it now relies on to justify
nonpayment.
First, Mr Beer says the solution was approved to
be moved to production.  Both words are telling.
"Approved" means the customer had authorised the
solution to proceed, and "production" means the live
operational environment.  This confirms that the
solution was put to use, and thus the very first event
of contractual occurrence occurred, contractual
acceptance occurred.
Muhammad, please you can close the screen.
Second, Microsoft acknowledges in its email dated
14 June 2023 relating to the gaps report, also sent by
Mr Beer, that what remained were roadmap items, future
enhancements, not contractual obligations under CR 37.
Mr Nassif, you will see the expression roadmap
repeatedly in the gaps report, and here it frequently
throughout this arbitration.  As the terms themselves
suggest roadmaps refer to items on the roadmap, not
contractual deliverable within Johnson Controls scope
under CR 37.  That is precisely why the terms does not
appear in the acceptance criteria of CR 37.
ARBITRATOR:  Can you take me through this 14th June 2023?
Can you please?  I read it.
I find it a little bit difficult for me to
understand your position here on that particular --
which I believe was C-29 before the bundle, you know,
pagination and numbering.
Can you please take this --
MS EID:  Yes, you mean the gaps report?
ARBITRATOR:  No.  The response to the gaps report of
14th June 2023.
MS EID:  Okay.
ARBITRATOR:  So your position, you said that the solution
has been tested, approved for production and used
during the World Cup and actively relied upon by
Intaleq through the BI dashboards.  That's the
position I need to look at C-29.  You can take me
through it.
MS EID:  So please, Muhammad, can you go back again to
{E90} and please scroll down.
So, Mr Nassif, this is the gaps report issued by
Intaleq to Microsoft and shared by Microsoft, by
Microsoft, shared with Johnson Controls on 1 June.
This document, if you can see the first two
categories, these are Intaleq comments.  But then when
Microsoft shared this document with us, it included in
it annotations and comments on its own.
So Mr Beer wrote his initial comments on the
report and sent it to us.  You can see in the third
table here Microsoft JCI feedback.  Those are the
initial feedback provided by Microsoft when it shared
the document with us.
And if you can scroll down.
If you go up, please.
Here you will see -- a bit more down, please.
Page 4, 5.
These are agreements, deliverables.
And here you can see, please, Muhammad, zoom in.
Mr Beer's comments saying, for example, for the
integration, this is a new requirement.  And for the
licence, Mr Beer says this is a separate agreement,
commercial agreement.
And if you go down on the roadmap again, please go
a bit down, Mr Muhammad, and just a bit you can see
here also mentioning for the gaps, Mr Beer is
mentioning, this is a new requirement document
evidence investigation, confirming that these are
either not within JCI scope or were closed.
And if you go a bit more down, you will see Andrew
Beer here, this is his comments.
Please zoom in, Muhammad, on the comment.  On the
comments.  Yes.
The pink comment.  Yes, please.
Mr Beer is asking JCI to provide feedback here.
So he provided feedback on behalf of both parties and
on behalf of Johnson Controls from his own knowledge
and confirmed that the items in table 1 which Intaleq
identifies our gaps are not gaps.  New features,
additional requirements.
And then can you please scroll to page 10.
Zoom in, please.  Yes.
You can see in blue Mr Beer's comments and
position on Intaleq statements.  So with Intaleq
mentioned in paragraph 3 that the scope delivered by
the FIFA was not fully delivered pending testing.
Please can you zoom in here.  Yes, this paragraph.
Until the start of the tournament and the business
stakeholders were unable to use a reliable,
well-tested solution.
This is here, Mr Nassif, the main document and the
main statement respondent relies on to allege that the
solution was not operational during the World Cup and
that we failed to deliver, noting that everything that
happened during the World Cup is not relevant to
CR 37, was closed in CR 37, as I will explain.
However, this is a statement, albeit irrelevant to
claimant's scope and claimant's claims, was inserted
by Intaleq in this report and Microsoft, Mr Beer
replied.  He replied by defending the solution and by
defending Johnson Controls.  You can see in blue
Mr Beer's commands.  He says the solution was tested
by Intaleq and approved to be moved to production on
29 September.
So he's telling Intaleq you are not correct.  The
solution was actually tested and approved by Intaleq
and moved to production and moved to production means
it moved to live or a live operational environment.
So the work is done, delivered.  The solution is
operational and it moves to production.
ARBITRATOR:  Thank you.  Thank you.
MS EID:  So just one note, Mr Beer in these comments.
And please, Muhammad, you can close the document.
And his comments on the gaps report where they are
roadmaps items.  He mentions that these are not a
commitment by Johnson Controls under CR 37 and in his
email dated 14 June 2023.
Again, Mr Beer confirms that the roadmap items are
not within claimant's scope under CR 37.  They are
additional requirements, enhancement requested by
Intaleq once for the future, for future use.
And as we will see, we've seen in our submissions
and you will see throughout this arbitration hearing,
the tribunal will find that the gaps report identifies
no CR 37 deliverables as incomplete and no failure to
satisfy the acceptance criteria of CR 37.
So if Microsoft genuinely believed that the gaps
report demonstrated a failure by Johnson Controls to
perform its obligations under CR 37, one would have
expected, at the very least, a rejection of the
relevant deliverables at any point or in a notice of
breach, at least after receipt of the gaps report.
Rather, Mr Beer defended the claimant's position
and no notice was ever issued.  Instead, Microsoft
continued to reassure Johnson Controls that payment
was forthcoming.
I will now address the obvious question: if
Johnson Controls performed, why did the customer never
pay?  The answer is again given by Microsoft and
Mr Beer -- thank you, Mr Beer.
So let me refer you to {C23} in November 2023,
after repeatedly assuring Johnson Controls that
payment was forthcoming, Mr Beer wrote -- and I quote:
"Intaleq have said that the only blocker to them
paying the invoices is confirmation of the
repatriation [issue]."
This is in November 2023, almost six months after
the gaps report in June 2023, so five to six months.
He's saying that the only blocker to payment is
not the gaps report, is not a failure to perform by
Johnson Controls, is not a non-operational solution.
But the issue of repatriation, which, as you will see
in the document, he acknowledges, is not within
claimant's scope.  It's a Microsoft obligation.
That explanation is not an isolated one.  It
appears consistently throughout the contemporaneous
record.  The reason is confirmed by Intaleq's own
contemporaneous correspondence, in which it repeatedly
makes clear that closure of the UNISTAD project was
conditional upon resolving the repatriation issue.
Could you please put {E93} on the screen, page 1.
Page 2, please.
Can you please scroll down a bit.
I'm not sure this is the document, but I will read
it.
It's an email from Intaleq, dated 10 May 2023 in
response.
{E92}, please.
This is an email.
Page 2, please.
Can you please zoom in.
Intaleq states -- and this is an email from the
customer Intaleq to Microsoft:
"The UNISTAD project was initiated with an
agreement to have it hosted out of QATAR before the
FIFA World Cup event, hence this was not met this is
seen as a project deliverable failure from Microsoft
side."
And if you scroll down, please, you will see that
in this email, Mr Beer was claiming payment,
requesting payment for the outstanding invoices.
So this email was in response to respondent's
request for Intaleq to pay claimant's outstanding
invoices that are now pending in this arbitration
Intaleq mentioned that unless you resolve the
repatriation issues, we will not -- which is a
Microsoft failure, we will not pay.
Thank you, Muhammad.  You can close.
Those words, Mr Nassif, leave no room for doubt.
Intaleq was not refusing to pay Johnson Controls or to
close the project because of any failure by Johnson
Controls as represented by respondent.  It was
refusing to do so because Microsoft had failed to
complete the repatriation, which is one of its main
obligations for the tribunal's benefit.  Repatriation
was the migration of the solution from Microsoft Cloud
Azure environment in Europe.
So there is a cloud environment.  This was not an
obligation or a service provided by Johnson Controls.
It was separately provided by Microsoft and initially
during the World Cup, Microsoft had the obligation to
secure that.  This is done from Qatar.  It failed.
And then Intaleq requested that at least after the
World Cup, the repatriation is done.  It wasn't done.
And that's why Microsoft noted a failure by Intaleq,
noted the failure by Microsoft.
And that's why throughout that period, Microsoft
was pushing claimant to provide this service, which is
outside its scope, free of charge, as a condition to
pay and to secure payment from Intaleq.
Finally, Mr Nassif, the use of the solution, the
customer's recent conduct speaks louder than any
allegation advanced in this arbitration.  It is
entirely inconsistent with Microsoft's case that the
solution was unusable, or that Johnson Controls failed
to perform under CR 37.
In fact, it has recently, only recently come to
our attention that the solution continued to be hosted
on the Microsoft Azure environment we spoke about
until May 2025.
So the license for Microsoft Azure, which would
have terminated in March 2023, was extended by Intaleq
to May 2025, two years after the closure of the
project.
Precisely to use the solution, the customer
renewed this license for two years and Microsoft knew
the solution remained live and operational.
This was never communicated to claimant, and the
question is, had the solution truly been defective or
unusable, Intaleq would have had no reason to keep it
running and incur substantial renewal costs.
It doesn't end here.  The customer then showcased
the solution at LEAP 2025 in Riyadh.  This is in
{E124} and LEAP 2025 is one of the largest technology
exhibitions in the world.
And the question here is that one is -- that what
one would expect of a customer disappointed,
disappointed with the fundamentally deficient solution
to exhibit it and promote it in a LEAP event?  And
again, it does not end here.  The customer has
recently approached Johnson Controls to assist in
reactivating the solution after the expiry of the
Microsoft Azure license.
Again, this is a rather curious way of treating a
subcontractor whose work is said to have been a
failure.
I turn quickly to the counterclaims, Mr Nassif,
and what we call here the grand awakening claims that
appear to have been discovered only after the notice
of arbitration was served.
At no point prior to the notice of arbitration,
nor during the project, nor during settlement had
Microsoft ever notified a breach, notified delay
damages or claimed any damages or compensation.  They
include 800,000 in alleged delay damages, 2 million in
alleged loss of revenue.  Indeed, for over two years
after project closure, claimant received no notices,
not even after the gaps report.
Then arbitration appeared, 60.7 million claim in
delay.  The claim was first 60.7 million and then
suddenly in two days it shrank to 800,000.  And the
claim for loss of revenue is very curious because this
is the profit respondent would have earned from
claimants from those 9 million unpaid invoices for
works performed and at a solution that is operational.
The facts did not change.  The project did not change,
only arbitration did.
And one note loss of revenue is expressly excluded
in the work order.  Yet, respondent still insists on
claiming it in this arbitration without any further
explanation.  Today, Microsoft asks the tribunal to
disregard every one of those contemporaneous
admissions.  But whichever version of events Microsoft
now advances, it leads to the same conclusion.  If
Microsoft genuinely believes, as its contemporaneous
documents repeatedly demonstrate, that Johnson
Controls had completed the project, then it failed to
fulfill its payment obligations.
If, on the other hand, it genuinely believed that
Johnson Controls had failed to perform, then it
equally failed in its obligations as the prime
contractor because it never communicated any alleged
breaches to Johnson Controls.  It never rejected the
milestone.  It reviewed and accepted the closure,
issued the closure report.  It disabled the claimant
access to the solution on the same day, thereby
preventing it from remedying any alleged defects and,
most importantly, it consistently maintained that the
only obstacle to payment was repatriation.
Mr Nassif, in fact, respondent was aware that the
solution was still in active use by the customer until
late 2025, and still chose to misrepresent the facts
in this arbitration.  These failures matter because
Microsoft knows that Johnson Controls has no
contractual relationship whatsoever with the customer
regarding its claims.  Microsoft knows that Johnson
Controls could not compel acceptance if it's not
secured by Microsoft.
Microsoft knows that Johnson Controls could not
recover directly.  It has no contractual relationship.
Microsoft knows that Johnson Controls could not
commence proceedings against Intaleq, only Microsoft
could.
Therefore, there is only one thing standing today
between Johnson Controls and payment is Microsoft and
the decision the esteemed tribunal will issue in this
arbitration.  Thank you.
ARBITRATOR:  Thank you very much, Ms Eid.  Thank you.
Thank you, Mr Roshan.  Shall we start with your
opening, please?  Thank you.
Opening submissions by MS ROSHAN
MS ROSHAN:  Thank you, Mr Nassif.
The case before you is, at its heart, a
straightforward one.
JCI was engaged by Microsoft to deliver the end
customer, Intaleq, a smart stadium that is a digital
management platform to connect all eight of the FIFA
World Cup stadiums into a single, unified smart
network.
The core service included essential digital
command centre, which is referred to as the C&CC, to
monitor, manage incidents, visualise reports,
dashboards and alarm management components across all
stadiums.  However, JCI did not deliver a solution
that worked.  It did not deliver a solution that
Intaleq, the end customer, was prepared to accept.
It was given a second chance after several delays
under amendment number 8, to close out a reduced and
simplified scope provision for a change initiated from
digital vault to OpenBlue, and to rectify a number of
defects.  It still did not deliver.
Having failed to meet its contractual obligations,
JCI now comes to this tribunal seeking payment as
though it had.  Microsoft respectfully submits that
JCI's claims must be dismissed in full, and
Microsoft's counterclaims for delay, damages and
direct loss of revenue should be upheld.
JCI opens this case by inviting the tribunal to
focus on a single document, Microsoft's notice of
breach, addressed to Intaleq dated 29 March 2024.  JCI
says this case begins and concludes with that
document.  Microsoft respectfully disagrees.
The case does not conclude with that document.
What followed tells the full story.  JCI's counsel
told the tribunal that when Microsoft wrote to its
customer, it took a clear position that JCI had
performed, that payment was demanded and that Intaleq
was in breach.  JCI says that that contradicts the
case Microsoft now advances.  It does not, and here is
why.
First, the notice must be read in context.
Microsoft, as prime contractor, was obliged to pursue
payments from Intaleq in respect of JCI milestones, as
Mr Beer confirms, because JCI failed to deliver the
solution.  Microsoft has never been paid by Intaleq,
despite the fact that Microsoft tried to assist JCI as
much as possible to close out the work order.  Mr Beer
addresses the 29 March 2024 notice at paragraph 64 of
his third witness statement.
Second -- and this is critical -- Microsoft did
not simply send the one notice.  Microsoft itself
refers to further requests for payment.  And third is
that Intaleq did not agree to pay.
So when JCI says this case begins and concludes
with the March 2024 notice, the tribunal should ask
this question, if JCI had truly performed its
obligations, and if Intaleq simply owed the money,
why, after multiple payment demands over the years,
across multiple escalating letters up to and including
a formal breach of contract notice, did Intaleq still
refuse to pay?  The answer confirmed by Intaleq itself
is that the solution was not capable of being used,
and that is seen in the gaps report.
I will address the tribunal on three broad topics
this morning.
First is the background to the dispute, told in
chronological steps that the evidence will later make
plain.
Second is Microsoft's defence to JCI's claims
addressing the contractual framework, the factual
record and the legal theories advanced by JCI, which
are all without merit.  And third is Microsoft's
counterclaims.
The background to this case can be summarised in
11 essential steps.  The first step is the contract.
The dispute arises from the Microsoft services
subcontractor agreement dated 3rd April 2019.
And for the transcript, this is bundle E, tab
{E1}, and the Microsoft services subcontractor work
order dated 24 December 2019.  For the transcript,
this is bundle E, tab {E2}.
JCI was engaged to deliver a smart digital
platform to connect the eight World Cup stadiums with
Intaleq as the end customer and Microsoft as prime
contractor to Intaleq.
Step 2 is JCI product change and the early warning
signs.  Microsoft had engaged JCI on the basis of
JCI's digital vault product, which JCI represented
itself would provide the required functionality.  This
can be seen in the work order.
If we could please turn to bundle E, tab {E2},
page 56.
And that's for the EP operator, please.
Here it says:
"Our proposed Digital Vault platform is uniquely
designed to ingest, store, and process
building-related data, and is already in use by global
enterprise customers.  Our deep understanding of
sensor placement, OT and IT system integration,
platform capability, and AI service give a significant
advantage in designing superior solution architectures
and implementation plans."
JCI subsequently, in February 2021, replaced the
Digital Vault with its OpenBlue product.  JCI did not
immediately notify Microsoft of this change.  It wrote
only to Intaleq.
JCI represented Intaleq that this was a simple
upgrade and rebrand.
And for the transcript, JCI letter is at bundle E,
tab E, page 1.
In November 2021, Microsoft raised concerns with
JCI regarding OpenBlue.
If we could please turn to bundle E, tab {E15}.
As can be seen in the first paragraph of this
letter, Microsoft informed JCI that while Intaleq had
been notified of the change to OpenBlue, no such
notification had been given to Microsoft, as can also
be seen in the third paragraph of this letter,
Microsoft recorded that the features described in the
statement of work for Digital Vault were not available
in OpenBlue.
And in paragraph 4, Microsoft flags delays on the
delivery timeline due to the development, with
OpenBlue to ensure that both JCI and Microsoft were
complying with their contractual obligations,
Microsoft requested JCI to confirm that all the agreed
features of Digital Vault are available in the
OpenBlue that for JCI to share the open Blue release
plan, in particular deliverables and timelines, and to
clarify the impact of replacing Digital Vault with
Open blue deliverables, features timelines.
Microsoft also noted the importance of informing
the customer of the change, seeking its approval and
amending the contract, but Microsoft's concerns were
not adequately addressed, and this product switch set
the tone for everything that followed.
Step 3 was the persistent delays and defective
performance within months of Microsoft raising
concerns regarding OpenBlue, Microsoft received
reports of further slippage and scope reductions
throughout the project.
Microsoft noted in correspondence that dates were
sleep slipping week after week.
If we could turn to bundle E, tab {E16}.
This is an email from Microsoft to JCI dated 17
December 2021.
Microsoft expressed its concern that the OpenBlue
product would not be ready to deliver on the contract
before the World Cup without significant executive
sponsorship and prioritization of resources on the JCI
side, and requested JCI for a plan to put the project
back to successful trajectory.
Despite Microsoft raising concerns, the delays
continued.
That can be seen in Microsoft's subsequent letter
of February 2022.
This is at bundle E, tab {E17}.
In this letter, Microsoft formally documented
major milestone delays caused by JCI and recorded that
the deployed versions were not sufficiently defect
free, functionally complete or stable.
In this letter, Microsoft also requested recorded
that JCI still had not responded to the concerns
raised in November 2021 regarding transition to
OpenBlue.
This can be seen in the last paragraph of that
letter.
If we could just scroll down.
Here, we can see that Microsoft expressly state
that they are still waiting for a response to the
issues raised in a letter dated 23 November 2021.
Step 4 is the negotiations for change request 37
in July 2022.  JCI initiated change request 37 to
formally record the change from Digital Vault to
OpenBlue.  However, change request 37 was not formally
concluded until after the World Cup.
And I will come back to this in step 6.
Step 5 is the World Cup and its failure by late
